body.heading: Thirty-six little futures
paragraphs: Two dice make 36 equally likely combinations, if you keep the dice distinct — imagine one red, one blue. The totals run from 2 to 12, but they are not equally likely, because some totals can be built in many more ways than others.

Twelve can only happen one way: 6 + 6. So can two: 1 + 1. But seven is a social number — 1 + 6, 2 + 5, 3 + 4, 4 + 3, 5 + 2, 6 + 1. Six combinations out of 36, a one-in-six chance on every roll, more than any other total.

body.heading: The hill in the middle
paragraphs: Count the combinations for every total and a hill appears: 2 and 12 have 1 way each; 3 and 11 have 2; 4 and 10 have 3; 5 and 9 have 4; 6 and 8 have 5; and 7 stands at the top with 6. The hill is perfectly symmetrical, because every pair of faces has a mirror pair that sums to 14 minus itself.

This is why board games and casino games treat seven as special, and why 'lucky seven' is not pure superstition — it is the hardest-working total on the dice. Games designers use this hill constantly, whether players notice it or not.

body.heading: Run your own tally
paragraphs: Test it: roll two dice 36 times and tally the totals in a table. Your results will not match the theory exactly — 36 rolls is a small sample — but seven should already be near the front of the pack, and the hill shape should be peeking through.

Roll another 36 and add the tallies together. Watching a wobbly small sample settle toward the true pattern, roll by roll, is the closest thing probability has to a magic trick — and you are performing it yourself.

takeaway: Seven wins because it has the most ways to happen — six of the thirty-six — not because the dice favour it.
